analysis.one_liner: Taxes opioid manufacturers a cent per milligram to fund addiction treatment and drug disposal, and tightens opioid marketing and prescribing rules.
analysis.headline: Introduced in July 2020 with zero cosponsors, the bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and died there without a hearing, a vote, or any further action when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would tax every milligram of opioid painkillers made in the United States, splitting the money between a national program to collect and safely dispose of leftover drugs and federal substance-abuse treatment programs. It would require drug company sales reps who market strong opioids to get a federal license with training and disclosure rules, force regulators to pull approval of opioids sold at ultra-high doses, and require doctors to complete pain-management training and check their state's prescription database before prescribing. It also would require Medicare to cover mental health and addiction treatment by telehealth, give states money to enforce equal insurance coverage for mental health and addiction care, and commission studies on covering non-drug back-pain treatments.
analysis.who_benefits: People at risk of opioid addiction and their families get prevention tools: fewer ultra-high-dose pills on the market, better-trained prescribers, and a national take-back program for leftover drugs. People with substance use disorders gain Medicare coverage of telehealth mental health care and state enforcement of equal insurance coverage for addiction treatment. Federal treatment programs gain a dedicated funding stream from the new opioid tax.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People at risk of addiction and patients in treatment

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a 1-cent-per-milligram excise tax on opioid manufacturers and splits the revenue between the Justice Department's national drug take-back program and SAMHSA substance abuse treatment block grants.

Requires federal licensure for pharmaceutical representatives who market schedule II opioids more than 15 days a year, with ethics training, a $3,000 fee, and annual disclosure of providers visited and gifts given.
Declares ultra-high-dose opioids — those exceeding CDC daily-dose guidelines — an imminent public health hazard and directs the Health Secretary to suspend their approval.

Requires prescribers of controlled substances to certify they completed federal pain-management and addiction training and registered with their state's prescription drug monitoring program before getting or renewing a DEA registration.
Expands Medicare telehealth coverage to diagnosis and treatment of mental health disorders and requires Medicare to reimburse mental health services delivered remotely.
Creates $10 million a year in grants to help states enforce mental health and addiction insurance parity, including audits and secret-shopper checks of insurers.
Conditions federal opioid grant money on states requiring prescribers to check prescription monitoring databases, dispensers to report fills within 24 hours, and cross-border data sharing.
Directs a National Academies study on whether Medicare should cover non-drug back-pain treatments such as acupuncture and exercise therapy, and whether lack of coverage drives opioid prescribing.

analysis.who_pays: Opioid manufacturers pay the excise tax on every milligram they produce and face lost sales from ultra-high-dose withdrawal and tighter prescribing. Drug makers bear the cost of licensing their opioid sales reps. Doctors who prescribe controlled substances bear new training and database-registration requirements. Health insurers face parity enforcement. Some of the manufacturer tax could be passed into drug prices for patients who legitimately need opioid pain relief.
analysis.who_pays_short: Opioid manufacturers, drug makers' sales arms, prescribers

drawbacks.text: The per-milligram manufacturer tax would likely be passed through to drug prices, raising costs for chronic-pain patients who use opioids responsibly under medical supervision.

Mandatory prescriber training, 72-hour-supply limits for noncompliant prescribers, and required prescription-database checks add administrative burdens on doctors and could make it harder for chronic-pain patients to fill legitimate prescriptions.

Forcing withdrawal of FDA approval for any opioid above CDC guideline doses removes a regulator's case-by-case judgment and could leave some severe-pain patients with no approved option at their dose.

The prescription monitoring provisions direct law enforcement access to patient prescription data and require states to submit lists of individual prescribers and dispensing amounts to federal agencies, raising surveillance and privacy concerns.
The parity enforcement, database, and reporting mandates are conditions on federal grants, effectively an unfunded requirement on states that rely on that money.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill aims squarely at a crisis that kills tens of thousands of Americans a year, and its heaviest costs fall on opioid manufacturers and marketers rather than patients. The honest trade-off is on the prescribing side: the same training limits and database requirements that prevent addiction also risk squeezing chronic-pain patients who depend on these medicines, and the automatic withdrawal of ultra-high-dose approvals leaves little room for exceptional cases. On balance the design targets the supply and marketing side of the epidemic more than patients, but it was never debated, so these trade-offs were never weighed in public.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in late July 2020, referred to the Senate Finance Committee, and the committee never took it up, so it died when the two-year Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Sen. Richard Durbin introduced the Addiction Prevention and Responsible Opioid Practices Act on July 21, 2020.
No senator — from either party — signed on as a cosponsor.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance, the committee with jurisdiction over the tax provisions.
No further action appears in the record: no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action, through the end of the 116th Congress on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Opioid manufacturers avoided a per-milligram tax, and their sales operations and prescriber customers avoided new licensing, training, and prescribing limits. Patients with pain and addiction got none of the bill's treatment and prevention provisions.

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.what_they_did: Sole sponsor; introduced the bill and spoke to it when it was read into the record.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred (chaired by Sen. Chuck Grassley, R-IA)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup, leaving the bill to die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Senate Republican majority
against.role: Held the majority and controlled the Senate floor calendar in the 116th Congress
against.what_they_did: Did not bring the bill to the floor; it received no floor action of any kind.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never drew a floor vote and drew zero cosponsors from either party, so its partisan shape was never tested; it originated with a single Democrat and died in committee.

industries.note: A 1-cent-per-milligram excise tax on production quotas, mandatory withdrawal of ultra-high-dose approvals, and reduced prescribing from prescriber training would directly cut revenue. The tax funds disposal and treatment programs that serve the public the industry's products harmed.

Reps promoting schedule II opioids would need a federal license with training, a $3,000 fee, and annual disclosure of every provider visited and gift given, raising the cost and visibility of opioid marketing to doctors.

industries.industry: Substance use disorder and mental health treatment providers
industries.note: Half the new opioid tax would flow to SAMHSA treatment programs, Medicare telehealth coverage of mental health and addiction care expands their patient base, and parity grants fund state enforcement that gets insurers to pay for their services.

State grants for parity compliance — audits, market conduct exams, secret-shopper programs — would force insurers to actually cover mental health and addiction treatment at rates equal to other care, and a GAO study targets coverage and reimbursement disparities.
Making Medicare telehealth coverage of substance use and mental health services permanent after the public health emergency locks in a remote-care market.

Schools receiving federal student aid would have to report annually on their pain-management and opioid-prescribing coursework, a light reporting burden that pushes prescriber education toward CDC guidelines.
